quiz.why: Wheezing requires airflow, so a silent chest in a patient working this hard means severe obstruction. This patient needs assisted ventilation, continued bronchodilator per protocol, and immediate ALS.

quiz.q: You are assisting a patient with a metered-dose inhaler. Which step sequence is correct?
choices: Inhale first, then press the canister, then exhale rapidly
Press the canister twice quickly, then breathe normally
Hold the inhaler two inches from the mouth and spray while exhaling
Shake the canister, exhale fully, seal the lips, press and inhale slowly, then hold for 10 seconds
quiz.why: The inhaled drug must travel deep into the airways on a slow, full inhalation and then be held there to deposit. Spraying during exhalation or firing two puffs at once deposits most of the dose in the mouth.

quiz.q: Which finding makes CPAP inappropriate for a patient in respiratory distress?
choices: A systolic blood pressure of 76 mmHg
Rales in both lung bases
A respiratory rate of 32
A history of congestive heart failure
quiz.why: CPAP raises intrathoracic pressure and reduces venous return, so hypotension is a contraindication. Rales, tachypnea and a heart failure history are exactly the picture CPAP is designed to treat.

quiz.q: Which statement about New Jersey BLS medication scope is most accurate?
choices: New Jersey EMTs may not administer naloxone
New Jersey EMTs may administer oxygen, oral glucose, aspirin, epinephrine and intranasal naloxone per NJ OEMS protocol
New Jersey EMTs may administer any medication the patient has at home
New Jersey EMTs may start IV lines for medication delivery
quiz.why: That list reflects the state's BLS scope, with epinephrine available by auto-injector or by syringe under an approved program and naloxone available to all levels of EMS. IV access is an ALS skill everywhere.

quiz.q: A 71-year-old on atenolol has been vomiting blood for two hours. His skin is cool and pale, capillary refill is 4 seconds, HR 76, BP 98/60. What is your interpretation?
choices: He is stable because his heart rate is normal
The beta blocker is masking compensatory tachycardia; treat him as being in shock
The atenolol dose should be repeated
Cool skin is expected in older adults and means nothing
quiz.why: Beta blockade prevents the heart-rate response to blood loss, so skin signs, capillary refill and mental status become the reliable indicators. A normal rate in a bleeding patient on a beta blocker is one of the most dangerous false reassurances in EMS.

quiz.q: Which medication on a patient's list should prompt you to ask about erectile dysfunction or pulmonary hypertension drugs before assisting with nitroglycerin?
choices: Metformin
Levetiracetam
Furosemide
Tadalafil
quiz.why: Tadalafil is a PDE-5 inhibitor sold as Cialis and Adcirca, and it contraindicates nitroglycerin for 48 hours. Metformin, levetiracetam and furosemide have no such interaction, though each tells you something about the patient's history.

quiz.q: A 33 lb child needs a weight-based dose. What is the weight in kilograms?
choices: 15 kg
22 kg
30 kg
73 kg
quiz.why: Divide pounds by 2.2: 33 divided by 2.2 equals 15 kg. That figure matters because 15 kg is the lower edge of the band where a 0.15 mg pediatric epinephrine auto-injector is used.

quiz.q: You must give 0.3 mg of epinephrine IM and pick up a vial labeled 0.1 mg/mL. What volume delivers the correct dose, and what should you check?
choices: 0.3 mL, and no further check is needed
3 mL, and you should verify whether your protocol intends the 1 mg/mL concentration for IM use
0.03 mL, drawn in a 1 mL syringe
1 mL, since concentration does not change the dose
quiz.why: Volume equals dose divided by concentration, so 0.3 divided by 0.1 is 3 mL. The 0.1 mg/mL concentration is the cardiac-arrest solution, so finding it in your hand for an anaphylaxis dose should stop you and make you verify the vial.

quiz.q: Medical control gives you a verbal medication order. What should you do before administering it?
choices: Administer immediately to save time and confirm afterward
Write it down and give it without speaking
Repeat the order back verbatim, including drug, dose and route
Ask your partner whether it sounds right
quiz.why: The verbatim read-back is the standard safety step and the moment errors in drug, dose or route are caught. It also creates a record on a recorded line of exactly what was ordered.

quiz.q: You withheld nitroglycerin because the patient took sildenafil that morning. How should this appear in your documentation?
choices: It should not be documented, since nothing was given
Record only that the patient refused
Note it in the vitals section as a blood pressure comment
Document that nitroglycerin was considered and withheld, and state the reason
quiz.why: Documenting what you considered and why you withheld it shows sound clinical reasoning, informs the receiving team, and protects you. Calling it a refusal misstates what happened.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 54M, 'acting drunk' at a bus stop
scenarios.intro: 1340 hours, clear and cold. Dispatch: 54-year-old male, confused, possibly intoxicated, reported by a passerby at a covered bus shelter. Police are on scene and report no violence and no weapons. You are staffed BLS with a glucometer, oral glucose, naloxone and oxygen. ALS is available with a 12-minute response.

steps.prompt: He is sitting on the bench, slumped to one side, eyes open, mumbling and not answering questions clearly. His shirt is soaked with sweat even though it is 38 degrees out. An officer says he smells no alcohol. There is a medical alert bracelet on his left wrist.

choices.text: Read the medical alert bracelet and check a blood glucose
choices.feedback: Correct. Diaphoresis with confusion and no alcohol smell screams hypoglycemia, and the bracelet is free history. Glucose is a vital sign in any altered mental status.

choices.text: Give 4 mg intranasal naloxone since he is altered
choices.feedback: No indication. His pupils, respiratory rate of 20 and saturation of 97 percent do not fit opioid overdose. Naloxone is for respiratory depression from opioids, not for altered mental status generally.

choices.text: Assume alcohol intoxication and offer a ride to the shelter
choices.feedback: Dangerous assumption, and the officer already told you there is no alcohol smell. Every altered patient gets a glucose check before any conclusion.

choices.text: Apply oxygen by nonrebreather at 15 L/min and transport immediately
choices.feedback: Oxygen is not indicated at a saturation of 97 percent, and leaving without checking glucose skips the one test that could fix him on scene. Oxygen is dosed to a target, not given reflexively.

steps.prompt: The bracelet reads 'Type 1 diabetic — insulin pump.' The glucometer reads `38 mg/dL`. He is now mumbling more and pushing your hand away, but he tracks you with his eyes, follows a simple command to open his mouth, and swallows his own saliva.

choices.text: Administer 15 g of oral glucose gel buccally, between the cheek and gum
choices.feedback: Correct. He is awake, follows a command and is swallowing, so he can protect his airway. Buccal placement is the right route, and 15 g is one full tube.

choices.text: Squirt the gel toward the back of his throat so it goes down faster
choices.feedback: That is how you cause aspiration. Oral glucose is placed between the cheek and gum where it absorbs through the mucosa, not deposited in the pharynx.

choices.text: Wait for ALS to arrive with IV dextrose rather than giving anything
choices.feedback: Twelve minutes of a glucose of 38 costs brain function, and he meets every criterion for the safe BLS option you already carry. Request ALS, but treat now.

choices.text: Give him a full can of soda to drink quickly
choices.feedback: A confused patient gulping liquid is an aspiration event waiting to happen, and the volume and sugar content are uncontrolled. Use the measured 15 g gel.

steps.prompt: Consider the alternative branch. Suppose instead that when you opened his mouth he was completely unresponsive to voice and pain, made no swallowing motion, and had no gag when you tested the airway with a suction tip.

choices.text: Manage the airway, position him laterally with suction ready, assist ventilation if needed, and request ALS for IV dextrose or glucagon
choices.feedback: Correct. No gag and no swallow means anything placed in the mouth ends up in the lungs. Airway first, then get the drug that does not need a functioning swallow.

choices.text: Place the glucose gel between the cheek and gum anyway, since it absorbs through the mucosa
choices.feedback: A common misconception. Buccal absorption is real but slow, and a patient with no airway protection will pool and aspirate the gel. Unresponsiveness is an absolute contraindication.

choices.text: Rub the gel on his gums with a gloved finger
choices.feedback: Same contraindication, plus you have put your fingers in the mouth of a patient who could seize or clamp down. Do not do it.

choices.text: Begin transport with the airway managed and meet ALS en route
choices.feedback: Reasonable if the intercept is closer than the hospital, though naming the airway plan explicitly is what makes it safe. Either way, no oral glucose.

steps.prompt: Back to the real patient, who did get the gel. Fourteen minutes later he is alert and oriented, apologetic, asking for a sandwich. Repeat glucose reads `96 mg/dL`. He says he feels fine and does not want to go to the hospital. He mentions his insulin pump 'has been acting up' since yesterday.

choices.text: Strongly encourage transport, explain that a malfunctioning pump can drop his sugar again, and contact medical direction about the refusal
choices.feedback: Correct. A continuing insulin source is an ongoing cause, so recurrence is likely. He has the capacity to refuse, but this refusal needs a real conversation and medical direction involvement.

choices.text: Accept the refusal, have him sign, and clear the call
choices.feedback: Too fast. He has a device still delivering insulin and an unexplained malfunction. Signing a form is not the same as informed refusal after a real risk discussion.

choices.text: Tell him he has no choice and must be transported
choices.feedback: An alert, oriented adult with capacity can refuse. Coercion is not a legal option, and it destroys the trust that persuasion depends on.

choices.text: Give a second tube of oral glucose so his sugar goes higher before you leave
choices.feedback: Not indicated at 96 mg/dL, and it treats your anxiety rather than his problem. The issue is the ongoing insulin delivery, not the current number.

steps.prompt: He agrees to go. You are writing the chart on the way in. Which entry is complete?

choices.text: '1348 — glucose 38 mg/dL. 1351 — oral glucose 15 g buccal per standing order. 1405 — alert and oriented, glucose 96 mg/dL, HR 88.'
choices.feedback: Correct and complete: the finding, the drug, dose, route, time and authorization, and a timed reassessment with the response. That is the six-item standard.

choices.text: 'Patient was hypoglycemic. Gave glucose. Improved.'
choices.feedback: Missing dose, route, times, authorization and objective reassessment. A narrative like this cannot support what you did if the call is ever reviewed.

choices.text: 'Gave one tube Glutose.'
choices.feedback: Trade name with no dose, route, time, authorization or response. Chart the generic name and all six items.

choices.text: 'Patient refused care, then accepted.'
choices.feedback: This records the disposition drama and none of the medicine. The glucose values and the medication record are the clinically important content.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern to carry: every altered mental status gets a glucose check, and the decision to give oral glucose turns entirely on airway protection — can he swallow and does he have a gag — not on how low the number is. When the answer is no, the drug changes to IV dextrose or glucagon and the intervention changes to airway management and ALS. Then there is the part people forget: fixing a number is not fixing a cause. An insulin pump still delivering insulin, or a long-acting sulfonylurea like glipizide, will drop him again after you leave, which is why that refusal deserved a real conversation and a call to medical direction. Finally, the chart: drug, dose, route, time, who authorized it, and a timed response. Six items, every time.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 7-year-old stung by a bee at a soccer field
scenarios.intro: 1620 hours, youth soccer practice at a town field. Dispatch: 7-year-old male stung by a bee, 'face is swelling up.' A coach says the boy's mother is on her way and that he has an EpiPen in his backpack. Your ambulance carries both adult 0.3 mg and pediatric 0.15 mg epinephrine auto-injectors, oxygen, a BVM, and albuterol per protocol. ALS is 9 minutes out.

steps.prompt: He is sitting on the grass surrounded by teammates, scratching at his neck. His lips and eyelids are visibly swollen, hives are spreading across his chest, and his voice sounds thick. He is breathing fast and you hear wheezing without a stethoscope. The coach says he weighs 'around 50 pounds.'

choices.text: Recognize anaphylaxis and prepare epinephrine immediately while your partner sets up oxygen
choices.feedback: Correct. Airway swelling plus wheezing plus hypotension is anaphylaxis by definition, and epinephrine is the only drug that treats all three. Every second of delay costs airway.

choices.text: Assist with albuterol first since he is wheezing
choices.feedback: Albuterol only opens the lower airways. It does nothing for the swelling closing his throat or for a blood pressure of 82/48. Epinephrine first, albuterol after if wheezing persists.

choices.text: Apply a cold pack to the sting site and monitor for 5 minutes
choices.feedback: This is a systemic reaction, not a local one. Watching a hypotensive child with a swelling airway for five minutes is how these calls end badly.

choices.text: Get a full history and allergy list from the coach before treating
choices.feedback: History can be gathered while you treat. With this presentation the indication is already met, and delaying epinephrine for paperwork is the wrong priority.

steps.prompt: Fifty pounds. You need to pick a device. Your bag has a `0.3 mg` adult auto-injector and a `0.15 mg` pediatric auto-injector. His own EpiPen Jr is in the backpack, expired last month.

choices.text: Convert: 50 divided by 2.2 is about 23 kg, which falls in the 15 to 30 kg band, so use the 0.15 mg pediatric device from your own supply
choices.feedback: Correct on both counts. The weight conversion puts him in the pediatric band, and you use your own in-date drug rather than his expired one.

choices.text: Use the 0.3 mg adult auto-injector since anaphylaxis is life-threatening
choices.feedback: The dose is weight-based for a reason. At about 23 kg the correct device is 0.15 mg; doubling it adds cardiac side effects without added benefit.

choices.text: Use his own EpiPen Jr because it was prescribed to him
choices.feedback: It is expired, which fails the three-check standard. Prescription ownership does not override an expiration date when you carry an in-date equivalent.

choices.text: Call medical direction to decide which device to use
choices.feedback: Calling costs time you do not have, and the weight-based choice is standing protocol. Give the pediatric dose now and notify while you work.

steps.prompt: You have the pediatric auto-injector out of the carrier. His shorts cover his thigh and he is squirming. A teammate is filming on a phone.

choices.text: Have the coach hold his leg still, press the device firmly into the outer thigh at 90 degrees through the shorts, hold per the device instructions, then massage the site
choices.feedback: Correct. Through clothing is explicitly acceptable, immobilizing the leg prevents a laceration from a moving needle, and massaging speeds absorption.

choices.text: Take time to remove his shorts and clean the skin with alcohol first
choices.feedback: Unnecessary delay. Auto-injectors are designed to fire through clothing, and in anaphylaxis the time cost is the risk, not the skin prep.

choices.text: Inject into the deltoid because the arm is easier to reach
choices.feedback: The vastus lateralis in the outer thigh has better blood flow and faster absorption. The deltoid is a slower site and a smaller target in a child.

choices.text: Hold the device against the thigh with your thumb over the tip for a firm grip
choices.feedback: Never. The needle fires from the tip, and thumbs have been injected this way. Grip the barrel in a fist with the tip facing the thigh.

steps.prompt: Six minutes after the injection: his hives are fading and the wheezing is quieter, but his voice is still thick, his lips remain swollen, and he says his throat 'feels tight.' He is shaking and says his heart is pounding.

choices.text: Give a second 0.15 mg dose per protocol for persistent airway symptoms, continue high-flow oxygen, and notify the hospital
choices.feedback: Correct. Repeat dosing at 5 to 15 minutes is indicated when symptoms persist, and continued throat tightness is an airway that has not been secured. Tremor and tachycardia are expected drug effects.

choices.text: Withhold further epinephrine because his heart rate is 158 and he is shaking
choices.feedback: Those are the drug working, not toxicity. Withholding epinephrine from a child with ongoing airway swelling because of expected beta effects is the classic fatal hesitation.

choices.text: Give the adult 0.3 mg device this time since the first dose was not enough
choices.feedback: Repeat the same weight-appropriate dose. Escalating to an adult device is not how repeat dosing works, and his weight has not changed.

choices.text: Start nebulized albuterol 2.5 mg for the residual wheezing and reassess
choices.feedback: Albuterol is reasonable as an adjunct for lower-airway wheeze per protocol, but it does not treat the throat tightness, which is the more dangerous finding. Epinephrine comes first.

steps.prompt: En route, he improves steadily. The throat tightness resolves, saturation reaches 98 percent, and he is chatting about the game. His mother meets you at the hospital and asks whether he really needed to be brought in, since he seems fine now.

choices.text: Explain that a biphasic reaction can return 4 to 12 hours later as the epinephrine wears off, so observation is required, and hand off both used devices with the times
choices.feedback: Correct. The biphasic risk is the reason every anaphylaxis patient is transported and observed, and the used devices with administration times are part of the handoff.

choices.text: Agree that he looks fine and support a decision to go home from triage
choices.feedback: Unsafe advice. Symptoms can return hours later, sometimes worse, and the family has no epinephrine now because his own device was expired.

choices.text: Tell her he needed it because it is required by law
choices.feedback: Deflection, and it does not help her understand the actual risk. Explain the biphasic reaction in plain words; families follow reasons better than rules.

choices.text: Say nothing and let the nurse explain it
choices.feedback: You were there for the reaction and you gave both doses. The handoff and the explanation of what you saw and gave are yours to deliver.

scenarios.debrief: Three decisions decided this call. First, recognition: airway swelling plus wheezing plus hypotension is anaphylaxis, and epinephrine is the only drug that reverses vasodilation, bronchospasm and swelling at once — albuterol, cold packs and antihistamines are adjuncts at best. Second, the dose: 50 pounds divided by 2.2 is about 23 kg, which lands in the 15 to 30 kg band, so 0.15 mg, and you used your own in-date device rather than his expired one. Third, the repeat: persistent throat tightness at six minutes meets the criteria for a second dose in 5 to 15 minutes, and a heart rate of 158 with tremor is the epinephrine working, not a reason to stop. The last piece is the biphasic reaction at 4 to 12 hours, which is why nobody with anaphylaxis stays home, however good they look in the driveway.
